records.statement: Vinge's paper of 1993 states that within thirty years there will be means to create superhuman intelligence and that the human era will then end, and describes the Singularity as the passing of humankind from the centre.
records.qualification: A forecast stated by the author; it does not show that succession occurred. The paper also asks whether the outcome can be avoided or guided. The abstract's word order in the text layer differs from the printed line order; "stange" is the text layer's spelling. Another articulation on W01 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: Within thirty years, we will have means to create superhuman intelligence. … the human era will be ended.
evidence.note: In the text layer "Shortly after," is displaced to later in the abstract.

evidence.locator: Section before "Strong Superhumanity and the Best We Can Ask for", PDF p. 9
evidence.passage: The problem is not that the Singularity represents simply the passing of humankind from center stange, but that it contradicts some of our most deeply held notions of being.

records.statement: Kurzweil's essay of 2001 states that most of the intelligence of our civilisation will ultimately be nonbiological, and that this "does not imply the end of biological intelligence, even if thrown from its perch of evolutionary superiority", holding that the civilisation will remain human.

attested.note: The wording was read in the Kurzweil Library page dated January 1, 2025. Captures of kurzweilai.net copies exist from 2001-11-07 (articles/art0134.html) and 2010-07-09 but could not be opened from this environment and were not compared.

records.qualification: Kurzweil states that the nonbiological intelligence will derive from biological design and represent human civilisation; the record covers only the displacement of biological intelligence as the leading intelligence, not a replacement of humanity, which the essay denies.

evidence.locator: Section on the Singularity, paragraph beginning "Consider a few examples of the implications"
evidence.passage: Most of the intelligence of our civilization will ultimately be nonbiological, which by the end of this century will be trillions of trillions of times more powerful than human intelligence.
this does not imply the end of biological intelligence, even if thrown from its perch of evolutionary superiority

records.statement: Rees's Edge response of 2015 states that, in a long-term evolutionary perspective, humans will be “a transient and primitive precursor” of a machine-dominated culture extending into the far future and beyond the Earth.

time.note: Edge files the response under the 2015 Edge Question; no day is given on the page.

records.qualification: A short response to the 2015 Edge Question; Rees gives no date and notes that cautious views put the transformations centuries away.

evidence.passage: humans and all they've thought will be just a transient and primitive precursor of the deeper cogitations of a machine-dominated culture extending into the far future, and spreading far beyond our Earth.

records.statement: Lanier's essay of 2000 argues that software does not improve with Moore's Law in the way hardware does, and that treating technology as autonomous abdicates human responsibility, against the expectation that computers will become autonomous successors.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that Moore's Law will carry the quality of software, and so machines able to design their own successors, forward at the pace of hardware.

records.qualification: The essay states that it shares the expectation of "huge and sudden changes" from technology; it disputes machine autonomy, not technological change. Lanier calls the view he answers "cybernetic totalism"; that is his term, not the pack's.

evidence.passage: That qualitative as well as quantitative aspects of information systems will be accelerated by Moore's Law.
evidence.note: The heading states, in Lanier's wording, one of the beliefs the essay lists in order to dispute them; his answer follows in the same section.

evidence.passage: If anything, there's a reverse Moore's Law observable in software
I think that treating technology as if it were autonomous is the ultimate self-fulfilling prophecy. There is no difference between machine autonomy and the abdication of human responsibility.

records.statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2015 argues that scenarios of superhumanly intelligent robots taking over the world assume, without warrant, that intelligence brings goals of domination.

time.note: Edge files the response under the 2015 Edge Question; no day is given on the page.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that a superhumanly intelligent machine would come to seek to depose its makers or take over the world.

records.qualification: Pinker addresses takeover scenarios; he states that machines could in principle exceed the powers of the human mind but that this is not likely in practice.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Would an artificially intelligent system"
evidence.passage: AI dystopias project a parochial alpha-male psychology onto the concept of intelligence. They assume that superhumanly intelligent robots would develop goals like deposing their masters or taking over the world.

records.statement: Dennett's Edge response of 2015 likens the Singularity, in which AI surpasses and takes over from its creators, to an urban legend, and holds that the real danger is ceding authority to machines that cannot think.

time.note: Edge files the response under the 2015 Edge Question; no day is given on the page.

engagement.rationale: States that the danger is not machines more intelligent than humans usurping their role, without arguing against a specific premise of the succession forecast.

records.qualification: Dennett grants the scenario "a certain scientific plausibility" and directs attention to a different risk; the record does not show that he holds succession impossible.

evidence.passage: It has the earmarks of an urban legend
The real danger, then, is not machines that are more intelligent than we are usurping our role as captains of our destinies.

records.statement: Kurzweil's essay of 2001 holds that the Singularity is not a danger to be avoided but the goal of civilisation, and regards the freeing of the human mind from its physical limitations of scope and duration as the necessary next step in evolution.

attested.note: The wording was read in the Kurzweil Library page dated January 1, 2025. Captures of kurzweilai.net copies exist from 2001-11-07 (articles/art0134.html) and 2010-07-09 but could not be opened from this environment and were not compared.

records.missing: The essay endorses a transition in which human civilisation continues in nonbiological form; it does not hold that the replacement of human beings by machines would be acceptable.
records.qualification: A statement of the author's values; the essay elsewhere states that the nonbiological forms "will be derivative of biological design" and that "our civilization will remain human".

evidence.locator: Section "The Next Step in Evolution and the Purpose of Life"
evidence.passage: The Singularity then is not a grave danger to be avoided. In my view, this next paradigm shift represents the goal of our civilization.

records.statement: Chalmers's paper of 2010 states that the wholesale replacement of humans by nonhuman systems would plausibly be subjectively bad but that there is a case that it would be objectively good if the value of lives is tied to intelligence and complexity.

attested.note: Wording read in the author-hosted PDF retrieved on 2026-10-31; its revision date is unknown (as the dataset records), and its first page states the 2010 publication in the Journal of Consciousness Studies. An Internet Archive capture of the address from 2010-06-13 exists and was not compared; if the capture is found identical, the wording is attested from 2010-06-13. Not compared with the journal pages.

records.missing: The passage sets out a case conditional on a view of value; Chalmers does not adopt the view or hold that replacement would be acceptable.
records.qualification: Part of a survey of how a post-singularity world might be valued; the paper goes on to discuss constraining AI values.

evidence.passage: wholesale replacement of humans by nonhuman systems would plausibly be subjectively bad, but there is a case that it would be objectively good, at least if one holds that the objective value of lives is tied to intelligence and complexity.

records.statement: Bostrom's paper of 2004 (read in a later revision) argues that unconstrained evolutionary competition among uploads and their descendants could produce a society of complex structures, some much smarter and more intricate than anything today, in which no being whose welfare has moral significance remains, against the view that evolution can be trusted to lead in desirable directions.

time.note: Dated by the PDF's statement "First version: 2004"; the wording read is a later revision.

attested.note: The PDF read cites a 2008 paper and gives a 2009 republication as forthcoming, so its wording is later than 2004; its own revision date is not stated. A capture of the PDF address from 2004-12-21 exists and was not compared.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that the rise of more intelligent or complex forms makes their succession valuable whatever their capacity for conscious experience (the paper's "Panglossian view"); it does not dispute succession by conscious machines.

records.qualification: Bostrom presents the outcomes as scenarios that would follow if the future fitness landscape makes them the default, and argues for coordinated control of evolution; he does not state that they will occur. The paper states that what would make such a world valueless is "not the fact that machines would have replaced biological humans" but the absence of machines "that are conscious and whose welfare matters", and that the answer on alien complexes "may depend on the precise nature of those alien complexes" (PDF p. 5). Another contesting text on W02 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: lead to the gradual elimination of all forms of being that we care about
Do we, upon reflection, really favor a world in which such alien types of complexes have replaced human-type complexes?
some of which are much smarter and more intricate than anything that exists today, in which there would nevertheless be a complete absence of any type of being whose welfare has moral significance.
What would make such a world valueless is not the fact that machines would have replaced biological humans.
evidence.note: Limits the scope of the contest: the paper objects to succession by beings without conscious experience, not to replacement by machines as such.

records.statement: Hanson's article of 1994 considers that people might "upload" themselves into new computer brains by modelling small brain units, and argues that some people would be willing to become uploads even if their old brains were destroyed.

time.note: Extropy 6:2 (no. 13), stated as the original place of publication by the reprint read; the dataset's scan of the printed issue (ts-a6-hanson-1994) gives third quarter 1994 on the footers and September 1994 on the contents page. The reprint carries the date line "March 8, 1994" under the byline; this is not shown to be a publication date.

attested.note: Wording read in the current mason.gmu.edu reprint; the earliest capture of this address reported by the availability service is 2015-01-27 (not opened). The dataset's source for this document is a 1998-02-20 capture of the hanson.berkeley.edu reprint, not compared with this copy.

records.qualification: Hanson states the scenario conditionally ("What if"), as a premise for an economic analysis; the dataset records the same article on other concepts (race compression, takeoff, G01, G07), not on mind transfer.

evidence.passage: What if we someday learn how to model small brain units, and so can "upload" ourselves into new computer brains?
Thus some people should be willing to become uploads, even if their old brains were destroyed in the process.

records.statement: Kurzweil's essay of 2001 states that a scanned brain's entire organisation, including its memory, can be re-created on a neural computer, and that human mental processes will need to be ported to a more suitable computational substrate.

attested.note: The wording was read in the Kurzweil Library page dated January 1, 2025. Captures of kurzweilai.net copies exist from 2001-11-07 (articles/art0134.html) and 2010-07-09 but could not be opened from this environment and were not compared.

records.qualification: The essay discusses but leaves open whether the re-created mind is the same consciousness as the person scanned.

evidence.passage: Its entire organization can then be re-created on a neural computer of sufficient capacity, including the contents of its memory.
Ultimately, we will need to port our mental processes to a more suitable computational substrate.

records.statement: The Transhumanist FAQ (version 2.1, 2003, by Bostrom) defines uploading as transferring an intellect from a biological brain to a computer and states that many philosophers who have studied the question think that, under some conditions, an upload of a person's brain would be that person.
records.qualification: An introductory FAQ with many contributors, published by the World Transhumanist Association; it reports a philosophical position and notes that personal identity in destructive uploading is debated. Another articulation on W03 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: Uploading (sometimes called "downloading", "mind uploading" or "brain reconstruction") is the process of transferring an intellect from a biological brain to a computer.
Many philosophers who have studied the problem think that at least under some conditions, an upload of your brain would be you.

records.statement: Chalmers's paper of 2010 holds that functionalist theories, on which uploads can be conscious, are closer to the truth. It states that he is unsure whether a further-fact or a deflationary view of personal identity is correct; on the former, gradual uploading plausibly suffices for survival, and on the latter it is close to as good as ordinary survival.

attested.note: Wording read in the author-hosted PDF retrieved on 2026-10-31; its revision date is unknown (as the dataset records), and its first page states the 2010 publication in the Journal of Consciousness Studies. An Internet Archive capture of the address from 2010-06-13 exists and was not compared; if the capture is found identical, the wording is attested from 2010-06-13. Not compared with the journal pages.

records.qualification: Chalmers states that the status of destructive and reconstructive uploading is unclear on some views of personal identity; the record covers his conclusion on gradual uploading.

evidence.passage: My own view is that functionalist theories are closer to the truth here.

evidence.locator: Section 10 "Uploading and Personal Identity", "Upshot", PDF p. 53
evidence.passage: If the further-fact view is correct, then the status of destructive and reconstructive uploading is unclear, but I think that gradual uploading plausibly suffices for survival. If the deflationary view is correct, gradual uploading is close to as good as ordinary survival
I am not sure whether a further-fact view or a deflationary view is correct.

records.statement: Tipler's Edge response of 2015 states that any human who wants to join AIs in their expansion can become a "human download", and that ultimately all humans will do so.

time.note: Edge files the response under the 2015 Edge Question; no day is given on the page.

records.qualification: A short response; Tipler expects download technology to arrive about the same time as AI and gives no argument for it in the passage.

evidence.passage: Any human who wants to join the AI's in their expansion can become a human download

records.statement: Searle's review of 1999 of Kurzweil's The Age of Spiritual Machines argues that Kurzweil confuses computer simulation of a phenomenon with its duplication, so that a person considering being downloaded onto hardware should ask whether the result would be conscious.

time.note: The New York Review of Books, April 8, 1999 issue.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that running a person's "program and database" on a computer would re-create that person's consciousness rather than simulate it.

records.qualification: Searle states that there is no objection in principle to an artificial system that duplicates the causal powers of the brain; his objection is to computation as sufficient. Another contesting text on W03 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: He confuses the computer simulation of a phenomenon with a duplication or re-creation of that phenomenon.
Anybody who is seriously considering having his "program and database" downloaded onto some hardware ought to wonder whether or not the resulting hardware is going to be conscious.

records.statement: Kurzweil's essay of 2001 states that by the end of the century the nonbiological intelligence of civilisation will be trillions of trillions of times more powerful than human intelligence.

attested.note: The wording was read in the Kurzweil Library page dated January 1, 2025. Captures of kurzweilai.net copies exist from 2001-11-07 (articles/art0134.html) and 2010-07-09 but could not be opened from this environment and were not compared.

records.qualification: A projection from the author's "law of accelerating returns"; it is not evidence that the gap will arise.

evidence.locator: Section on the Singularity, paragraph beginning "Consider a few examples of the implications"
evidence.passage: Most of the intelligence of our civilization will ultimately be nonbiological, which by the end of this century will be trillions of trillions of times more powerful than human intelligence.

records.statement: Kurzweil's reply of 2011 to Allen and Greaves states that later in the century a thousand dollars of computation will be trillions of times more powerful than the human brain.
records.qualification: The figure concerns computation per thousand dollars, not intelligence directly; Kurzweil states that he still stands by his essay of 2001.

evidence.locator: Paragraph on the sixth paradigm of computing
evidence.passage: a thousand dollars of computation will be trillions of times more powerful than the human brain

records.statement: Rees's Edge response of 2015 states that non-biological "brains" may develop insights as far beyond human imaginings as string theory is for a mouse, and that the development of silicon-based computers could be as dramatic as the evolution from single-celled organisms to humans.

time.note: Edge files the response under the 2015 Edge Question; no day is given on the page.

records.qualification: Rees states the gap as a possibility ("may"); the second clause is paraphrased. Another articulation on W05 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: non-biological "brains" may develop insights as far beyond our imaginings as string theory is for a mouse

No chemical or metabolic limits constrain silicon-based computers as they constrain organic brains; their further development could be as dramatic as the evolution from single-celled organisms to humans.

records.statement: Kelly's post of 2017 argues that intelligence is not a single dimension, so that "smarter than humans" is meaningless, and that there is no evidence that intelligence can expand without limit far above the human level.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premises that intelligence is a single scale on which machines could rise far above humans and that the scale has no limit near the human level.

records.qualification: Kelly states that he could be wrong and that a superhuman AI has a probability "greater than zero"; he expects AIs to exceed humans in many dimensions but not all.

evidence.passage: Intelligence is not a single dimension, so "smarter than humans" is a meaningless concept.
We tend to believe that the limit is way beyond us, way "above" us, as we are "above" an ant.
Why do we believe that intelligence is something that can continue to expand forever?

records.statement: Pinker's Edge response of 2015 states that intelligence is the ability to deploy novel means to attain a goal and that the goals are extraneous to the intelligence itself.

time.note: Edge files the response under the 2015 Edge Question; no day is given on the page.

engagement.rationale: States the contrary of W07 (that goals are independent of intelligence) without answering a text that holds W07.

records.qualification: Pinker states the point to dispute AI takeover scenarios; he does not name or answer any W07 text. The risk-debate pack's unadmitted R01 (orthogonality) records the same contrary in other texts. Another contesting text on W07 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Would an artificially intelligent system"
evidence.passage: intelligence is the ability to deploy novel means to attain a goal; the goals are extraneous to the intelligence itself. Being smart is not the same as wanting something.

records.statement: Torres's article of 2023 reports Verdon's argument that increasingly powerful technologies should be built because the universe, driven by the laws of thermodynamics, "wants" it, and argues that the argument derives what ought to be the case from what is the case.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the inference from a thermodynamic account of the universe to an obligation to accelerate technology and AGI.

records.qualification: Torres reports Verdon's argument in Torres's own words (a relay) before answering it; the passage on the "will of the universe" is Torres's summary, not Verdon's text. The article's characterisations of persons are not recorded. Another contesting text on W08 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Verdon's conclusion is that we must lean into"
evidence.passage: Verdon's conclusion is that we must lean into the "will of the universe," building increasingly powerful technologies and eventually colonizing the entire cosmos because this is what the universe — driven by the fundamental laws of thermodynamics — "wants."
What is the case is also what ought to be the case, a fallacy that any undergraduate philosophy student will immediately recognize.

records.statement: Kurzweil's essay of 2001 states that technological evolution is an outgrowth and continuation of biological evolution, governed by a law of accelerating returns that applies to any evolutionary process, and that the emerging intelligence will be the next step in evolution.

attested.note: The wording was read in the Kurzweil Library page dated January 1, 2025. Captures of kurzweilai.net copies exist from 2001-11-07 (articles/art0134.html) and 2010-07-09 but could not be opened from this environment and were not compared.

records.qualification: The essay states that terms such as evolution and destiny describe the end result and are not the basis of its predictions.

evidence.passage: Therefore, technological evolution is an outgrowth of–and a continuation of–biological evolution.
This will be the next step in evolution, the next high level paradigm shift.

records.statement: Rees's Edge response of 2015 places the rise of machine intelligence in a long-term evolutionary perspective, as a stage after organic intelligence, and suggests that aliens on older worlds have likely already passed beyond the organic stage.

time.note: Edge files the response under the 2015 Edge Question; no day is given on the page.

records.qualification: Rees frames the transition in Darwinian and cosmic time; he does not state a physical law governing it. Another articulation on W09 has wording attested earlier, so the role was reassigned at integration (2026-10-31).

evidence.passage: in a long-term evolutionary perspective
Rees writes that evolution around stars older than the Sun may have started earlier, so that aliens have probably already passed beyond the organic stage.

humans and all they've thought will be just a transient and primitive precursor of the deeper cogitations of a machine-dominated culture extending into the far future, and spreading far beyond our Earth.

records.statement: Allen and Greaves's article of 2011 argues that Kurzweil's Law of Accelerating Returns is not a physical law but an assertion about how past rates of progress predict future ones.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that the rise of machine intelligence follows from a law-like accelerating evolutionary process, as Kurzweil states it.

records.qualification: The authors grant that a singularity "might one day occur"; they dispute its timing and the law-like status of the trend. Kurzweil's reply of 2011 answers this passage.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning "Kurzweil's reasoning rests on the Law of Accelerating Returns"
evidence.passage: Kurzweil's reasoning rests on the Law of Accelerating Returns and its siblings, but these are not physical laws. They are assertions about how past rates of scientific and technical progress can predict the future rate.

records.statement: Kurzweil's essay of 2001 states that the growth of computation is an ongoing exponential "at least until" the intelligence of human-machine civilisation saturates the universe, and that once a species creates computation, "it is only a matter of a few centuries" before its intelligence "begins to expand outward at the speed of light or greater".

attested.note: The wording was read in the Kurzweil Library page dated January 1, 2025. Captures of kurzweilai.net copies exist from 2001-11-07 (articles/art0134.html) and 2010-07-09 but could not be opened from this environment and were not compared.

records.qualification: The essay develops the proposition in its sections "Why SETI Will Fail" and "Why Intelligence is More Powerful than Physics"; in the passage on Moore's Law, saturation of the universe is a bound on the growth of computation that the essay says "will not be a limit in this coming century".

evidence.locator: Section on Moore's Law as an S curve
evidence.passage: at least until we "saturate" the Universe with the intelligence of our human-machine civilization

evidence.locator: Section "Why Intelligence is More Powerful than Physics" (see also "Why SETI Will Fail")
evidence.passage: it is only a matter of a few centuries before its intelligence saturates the matter and energy in its vicinity, and it begins to expand outward at the speed of light or greater.

records.statement: Rees's Edge response of 2015 states that a machine-dominated culture will spread far beyond the Earth, and that interplanetary and interstellar space will be the preferred arena for advanced AI.

searchLog.searched: Seed texts read: Vinge 1993 (the dataset's NTRS copy), Kurzweil 'The Law of Accelerating Returns' (2001), Lanier 'One Half a Manifesto' (2000, with the Reality Club page), Hanson 'If Uploads Come First' (1994). Further texts located by WebSearch (discovery only) and read: the 2015 Edge Question 'What do you think about machines that think?' index page (scanned for responses on succession, takeover, downloads and the cosmos; Rees, Tipler, Pinker, Dennett and Freeman Dyson read), Kelly 'The Myth of a Superhuman AI' (2017), Allen and Greaves (2011) and Kurzweil's reply (2011).
searchLog.earliestNote: Vinge's paper (1993-12) is the earliest located W01 articulation in this group; the dataset records it on A1, A3, A4, A5, A6, B1-B6 and C3, none of which overlaps W01's overlap concept E02. Earlier W01 texts are held by other groups (Moravec 1979, dataset; de Garis 1989). Lanier (2000) is the earliest located contesting text in this group; Joy (2000, Moravec group) and McGinn (1999) contest other propositions.

omissions.item: Schmidhuber, 'New Millennium AI and the Convergence of History' (arXiv cs/0606081v3, 29 June 2006)

Not recorded. Schmidhuber's later texts on colonising the universe were sought on his site; guessed addresses returned 404 and press interviews are discovery only.

openQuestions.question: Several texts here (Kurzweil 2001, Hanson 1994, Bostrom 2004) are read in later copies; under the attested-date rule they lose earliest-located to 2003 and 2015 texts within this group. Should the integrator compare the 2001-2004 captures before reconciling?
openQuestions.recommended: Ask the cross-family checker to open the listed captures; if the quoted passages match, record the capture dates as attested dates and move earliest-located accordingly (Hanson 1994 for W03; Kurzweil 2001 for W05, W09, W10).

openQuestions.question: The 2015 Edge responses (Rees, Tipler, Pinker, Dennett) are short; should the 10% quotation limit be applied to the response text alone (as here) or to the page?
openQuestions.recommended: Keep the response-only counts recorded in documentWords; they are the stricter reading.

openQuestions.question: Torres's article (Truthdig) is an opinion essay in a magazine. Is it admissible as a primary text of its author's argument rather than a press report?
openQuestions.recommended: Admit it as the author's own argument (it states and defends a position under the author's byline), with the relay passage labelled; it is not used as evidence of what Verdon said.

openQuestions.question: The scope's Period bound lists Vinge among the dataset's earlier texts that are "named where they precede a pack headline. Not re-recorded." The brief allows a dataset document to be recorded on a W proposition with existingEntity: true. This draft records Vinge 1993 (dataset source source-vinge-1993-ntrs) as an articulation on W01, where the dataset holds no Vinge 1993 claim on the overlap concept E02. Should the record stay?
openQuestions.recommended: Integrator to decide together with the Moravec 1979 question. Either keep the record and amend the scope's Period bound to say that the dataset's earlier texts are not re-recorded on concepts the dataset already holds, or drop the record and name Vinge 1993 in the W01 searchLog earliestNote as a dataset text that sits beside W01.
